questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the system that makes a governance decision actually happen day to day — where definitions live, what enforces them, how a change propagates — is called governance ________.
questions.explain: Governance architecture is the technical system that implements a governance decision. Governance is the decision itself (who holds authority, what's classified how); governance architecture is what makes that decision real across dozens or hundreds of platforms.

questions.prompt: Which statement below correctly matches one of this course's five core governance-architecture principles to its actual meaning?
options: Single source of truth per concept means every business concept must be stored in exactly one physical database, with no replication anywhere.
Single source of truth per concept means any given business concept should have exactly one authoritative definition and location that other systems reference, even if it's physically replicated.

Separation of concerns means the metadata layer, policy layer, and the underlying data storage should all be combined into one single, tightly integrated system, so changing any one of them always requires changing all three together.
Automate enforcement, don't rely on memory means every governance rule must be automated immediately, with no exceptions ever logged.
Design for loose coupling means platforms should connect through tight, platform-specific integrations tailored to each individual pairing.
Data as a shared asset means data belongs to whichever team produces it, and other teams must request a copy through that team.
questions.explain: Single source of truth per concept means exactly one authoritative definition and location that other systems reference — it explicitly allows physical replication, as long as there's one authoritative source being referenced. Separation of concerns means keeping those layers architecturally distinct, not combined; loose coupling means defined interfaces, not tight platform-specific integration; and data as a shared asset means data belongs to the organization, not to the producing team.
questions.distractorExplain: Option A reuses the exact same principle name and sounds nearly identical, but swaps one meaningful detail: it claims the concept must be stored in exactly one physical database with no replication anywhere. The real principle explicitly allows physical replication — what matters is having one authoritative definition and location that other systems reference, not forbidding every copy.

questions.prompt: Match each governance reference-architecture pattern to its correct description.
right: A single central metadata hub connects to every platform, pulling metadata, lineage, and classification into one place
Each domain or platform runs its own catalog; a lighter-weight central index registers where each domain catalog lives and what it covers
Fully distributed discovery through shared standards, with no central index at all
questions.explain: Hub-and-spoke centralizes detail in one hub; catalog-of-catalogs keeps detail in domain catalogs with only a lightweight central index; mesh of catalogs has no central index at all, relying entirely on shared standards for discovery.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement below about the governance capabilities map, per this course.
options: A capability map is independent of org chart or specific tooling — it describes what an organization needs to be able to do
Two organizations running the same operating model always have identical capability maturity
Lineage tracking and cataloging/discovery are both among the eight governance capability domains
Data quality management and stewardship workflow are two of the eight capability domains
A capability rated 'present but manual' is treated identically to one rated 'absent' when auditing an organization
questions.explain: The capability map is deliberately independent of org chart and tooling, and includes lineage tracking, cataloging/discovery, data quality management, and stewardship workflow among its eight domains. Two organizations with the same operating model can still have very different capability maturity — the map is a different lens from the operating-model question. And 'present but manual' is a distinct rating from 'absent,' not an equivalent one.

questions.prompt: An organization runs a genuinely federated operating model, but its architecture team builds one centralized hub that holds every domain's full metadata detail directly, with domain teams expected to request any change through the central team. What's the architectural problem here, per this course?
options: This is an architectural mismatch — a true hub-and-spoke architecture centralizes detail and undermines the local autonomy a federated operating model is supposed to preserve
There is no problem — any reference architecture pattern works equally well with any operating model
This is deliberate decentralization, which is an architecturally sound choice for this scenario
This is federated computational governance, since a central team happens to be involved
questions.explain: You cannot bolt a fully centralized hub-and-spoke architecture onto a genuinely federated operating model without undermining the autonomy that model is supposed to preserve. A federated model architecturally pairs with catalog-of-catalogs, where domain catalogs retain real authority over their own detail — not a hub that holds everything directly.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: centralized governance architecture needs three components — a single enterprise metadata hub, a single policy engine, and a single ________, where every access request routes through the same central team and approval process.
questions.explain: The access-provisioning queue is the third component: every access request, to any data on any platform, routes through the same central team and the same approval process — which is also exactly where the centralized model's bottleneck shows up as request volume grows.

questions.prompt: Three business units each independently bought their own catalog tool over several years with no coordination, resulting in incompatible classification tags across units. Per this course, is this deliberate or accidental decentralization, and why?
options: Accidental — nobody designed a shared layer on purpose; this kind of incompatibility is simply what happens when no one architects anything deliberately
Deliberate — because each business unit had the organizational authority to choose its own tool
Deliberate — because incompatible classification tags are a necessary tradeoff of any decentralized model
Accidental — but only because the three units happen to operate in different countries
questions.explain: Deliberate decentralization is a conscious choice made because business units are genuinely unrelated and nothing needs to cross their boundary. This scenario — no one designed anything, incompatible tags accumulated as a side effect — is accidental decentralization, the far more common default state when no one architects a shared layer on purpose.

questions.prompt: Select every one of data mesh's four stated principles, per this course.
options: Domain-oriented decentralized data ownership and architecture
Data as a product
Self-serve data infrastructure as a platform
Federated computational governance
Centralized access-provisioning queue
Mandatory single enterprise metadata hub
questions.explain: Data mesh's four principles are domain-oriented decentralized ownership, data as a product, self-serve infrastructure as a platform, and federated computational governance. A centralized access-provisioning queue and a mandatory single enterprise metadata hub both belong to the centralized model instead, which mesh deliberately avoids.

questions.prompt: Match each data-product characteristic to its correct description, per this course.
right: Shows up in a catalog, with enough description that someone outside the producing team can find it
Has a stable, known way to be accessed that doesn't change out from under consumers
Its quality is known and communicated, not assumed
Access control travels with the product itself, not bolted on afterward by whoever consumes it
questions.explain: A data product earns the name by being discoverable (findable in a catalog), addressable (a stable access point), trustworthy (known, communicated quality), and secure (access control travels with it) — alongside self-describing and interoperable, the other two characteristics this course names.

questions.prompt: A mid-size insurance company has three domains: claims and underwriting share a real cross-cutting need for consistent regulated data, while marketing's data is largely independent. The capability map shows decent metadata management but weak lineage and no shared schema, and there's no budget yet for a self-serve data platform. Per this course's architectural factors, which model fits best?
options: Federated governance, scoped narrowly to claims and underwriting's regulated data, with marketing left running its own separate architecture for now
Full data mesh across all three domains immediately, since mesh is the most advanced model available
Fully centralized governance across all three domains, since centralization always guarantees the most consistency
Fully decentralized governance everywhere, since marketing's data doesn't cross-cut with the other two
questions.explain: With no budget for a self-serve platform, data mesh isn't realistic yet — choosing it without that investment produces decentralization with mesh vocabulary. Claims and underwriting's genuine cross-cutting need points to federated governance scoped to them specifically, while marketing, with no cross-cutting need, can stay separately governed.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a source system actively emitting a metadata event the moment something changes, rather than waiting for a scheduled scan, is called ________ harvesting.
questions.explain: Push-based harvesting means the source system emits a metadata event the instant something changes, usually via an API call or message queue — far more real-time than pull-based crawling, but it requires every source to cooperate and emit events the receiving store understands.

questions.prompt: Why is the connector layer, not the UI, usually the deciding factor in a catalog build-vs-buy decision, per this course?
options: Because writing and maintaining reliable connectors against dozens or hundreds of source-system types is the genuinely expensive part, and a vendor has already built and tested that across many customers
Because catalog UIs are technically impossible to build without purchasing a vendor license
Because connectors are cheap to build but search UIs require specialized licensed technology no organization can build itself
Because every catalog vendor charges separately for UI access, making it the single most expensive component
questions.explain: Writing and maintaining reliable connectors against many different source-system types — each with its own API, schema quirks, and rate limits — is the genuinely expensive part of a catalog. A vendor has already built and tested that across many customers, which is why most organizations adopt a catalog platform rather than building one.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement below about lineage architecture, per this course.
options: Table-level lineage records that one table was built from another, without tracing individual fields
Column-level lineage is generally cheaper to capture than table-level lineage
Query log parsing reconstructs lineage after the fact from a system's existing SQL query history
Runtime instrumentation captures dynamic transformation logic that static code parsing would miss
OpenLineage is a proprietary specification owned by a single vendor
questions.explain: Table-level lineage is coarse, tracking whole tables. Query log parsing works retroactively from existing SQL history. Runtime instrumentation captures dynamic logic that static parsing would miss. Column-level lineage is dramatically more expensive to capture than table-level, not cheaper — and OpenLineage is an open, vendor-neutral specification, not a proprietary one.

questions.prompt: Match each catalog-integration pattern to its correct description, per this course.
right: One top-level catalog pulls metadata from each platform-native catalog through its own connectors into one combined search surface
The central catalog periodically copies each platform's metadata on a schedule, which can drift stale between pulls
The central catalog queries each platform's catalog API live at search time and merges results, avoiding staleness at the cost of latency
questions.explain: A federation hub pulls metadata through its own connectors into one combined surface. Pull-based synchronization copies metadata on a schedule and can go stale between pulls. API-based federated search queries live at search time, trading staleness for latency and dependence on every platform's API being up.

questions.prompt: A column gets tagged sensitive, and a masking policy already attached to that tag applies automatically to every future query against it, with no human reviewing each query first. Per this course, is this passive or active metadata, and why?
options: Active metadata — the tag triggers automated enforcement the moment a query runs, with no human required for the triggering step
Passive metadata — because a human originally applied the sensitivity tag before any automation happened
Active metadata — but only because the masking policy happens to be stored in the same database as the catalog
Passive metadata — because masking only hides data, so it doesn't count as an automated action
questions.explain: The distinction isn't about what the metadata says or who applied the original tag — it's about whether something downstream actually acts on it automatically. Here, the masking policy fires automatically on every query the moment it runs, with no human in the triggering step, which is exactly what makes it active metadata.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: an access-control model where access is decided by evaluating attributes of the user, the data, and the request context at the moment access is requested — rather than through a fixed role — is called ________.
questions.explain: ABAC (attribute-based access control) evaluates attributes at request time, so no new role is needed for every fine-grained combination — the tradeoff is policy logic that's harder to audit just by reading a list of role names, which is why RBAC still handles the coarse grain in most real architectures.

questions.prompt: Which statement below correctly describes where access-control enforcement is architecturally strongest, per this course?
options: Query-time (engine-level) enforcement is strongest, because the policy is defined once and applies no matter which tool issues the query — a dashboard, notebook, or ad hoc SQL client all get the same result.
Query-time (engine-level) enforcement is strongest, because it is always faster to implement than filtering results inside an application.
Application-time enforcement is strongest, because a dedicated BI tool can apply more sophisticated filtering logic than a database engine ever could.
RBAC alone is always sufficient, since attribute-based rules add unnecessary complexity to any real governance system.
Enforcement location doesn't matter, since any policy enforced anywhere in the stack provides equivalent protection.
Application-time enforcement is strongest, because it protects data regardless of which tool a user connects with.
questions.explain: Query-time enforcement is architecturally stronger because it's defined once, centrally, and applies no matter which tool issued the query. Application-time enforcement only protects users going through that one specific application — anyone with direct query access to the underlying engine bypasses it entirely, the opposite of option F's claim.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B reaches the same conclusion as the correct answer — query-time enforcement is strongest — which makes it the tempting pick. But it swaps out the actual reason: the lesson's point is that query-time enforcement applies no matter which tool issues the query, not that it's 'faster to implement.' Implementation speed was never the stated reason, and in practice query-time enforcement often takes more upfront engineering than an application-level filter.

questions.prompt: Given this Rego policy, can a user whose role is "analyst" access a resource tagged classification: "confidential"?
options: No — access to a confidential resource is only allowed when the user's role is specifically data-steward; neither allow rule matches an analyst requesting confidential data
Yes — the default allow := false line is automatically overridden for any authenticated user
Yes — the first allow rule permits any user as long as the resource has a classification tag at all
It depends on whether the resource also has an owner tag set, which this policy also checks
questions.explain: The first allow rule only matches when classification is NOT "confidential" — it doesn't apply here. The second allow rule requires both classification == "confidential" AND role == "data-steward" — an analyst fails that second condition. With no matching allow rule, the default allow := false stands, so access is denied.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement below about governance automation, per this course.
options: CI/CD pipeline checks run an automated policy check against a proposed change before it's allowed to merge
Scheduled compliance scans catch policy drift caused by manual changes made outside any pipeline
Event-triggered checks fire immediately on a change event, closer to real time than a scheduled scan
Most real governance automation architectures start with automated remediation and move to detection-only over time
Automated remediation means the system fixes a detected violation itself, with no human in the loop at the moment of the fix
questions.explain: CI/CD checks run before a merge, scheduled scans catch drift from manual out-of-band changes, and event-triggered checks fire in near real time. Automated remediation means the system fixes the violation itself with no human in the loop. Most architectures actually start with detection-only and move to remediation over time — the reverse of what the false statement claims — specifically because a wrong automated fix with no human review can cause its own outage.

questions.prompt: Match each platform to how far its governance reach extends, per this course.
right: Governs what happens inside its own engine only
Governs across many workspaces of its own platform, even across clouds, but still within its own compute
Governs across several of its own workload types because they all share one tenant-wide lake
Governs across other vendors' platforms entirely, since its job is to reach into other systems' metadata
questions.explain: Snowflake's governance is engine-native and narrowest. Unity Catalog spans Databricks workspaces, even across clouds, but stays within Databricks compute. Fabric spans several workload types because they share OneLake. Purview has the widest reach, explicitly built to reach into other vendors' platforms entirely.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a short, dated document capturing one specific architecture decision — the context that made it necessary, what was decided, and its consequences — is called an ________.
questions.explain: An ADR (architecture decision record) is a short, historical record written once at the time of a decision and rarely edited afterward — a later change gets its own new ADR, not an edit to the old one.

questions.prompt: A governance team builds a polished strategy slide deck, presents it once to leadership, gets a round of approving nods, and never produces a roadmap, budget line, or named owner from it. Per this course, which strategy failure mode is this?
options: The strategy becomes a slideshow — a polished deck presented once and never translated into a roadmap, budget line, or owner
No sponsor, no budget, no strategy — the specific failure of lacking an executive sponsor
Trying to govern everything at once — the failure of attempting centralized governance over every domain simultaneously
A capability map problem — the organization rated too many of its own capabilities as absent
questions.explain: This is exactly 'the strategy becomes a slideshow': a polished deck presented once, approved, and never referenced again because it was never translated into a roadmap, a budget line, or a named owner.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement below about governance and architecture roadmaps, per this course.
options: A roadmap turns a strategy's priorities into a time-ordered sequence people can actually plan against
The Now/Next/Later horizon structure avoids over-committing to precise dates far in the future
A roadmap that is entirely foundational work tends to lose executive patience before it shows value
Dependency mapping is optional, since roadmap initiatives never actually depend on each other
A roadmap without a strategy behind it still supplies its own 'why' and 'what'
questions.explain: A roadmap sequences a strategy's priorities into a real timeline, and Now/Next/Later deliberately avoids over-precise future dates. All-foundational roadmaps lose executive patience before showing value. Dependency mapping is explicitly not optional — skipping it produces initiatives that stall when a silent dependency isn't done. And a roadmap without a strategy is just a backlog with dates; the strategy supplies the why and what, not the roadmap.

questions.prompt: Put these four questions a governance strategy document must answer in the order this course presents them.
items: Where are we now? An honest maturity assessment against the capabilities map
Where are we going, and why? The target state tied to a real business outcome
What do we build first, and in what order? A small number of sequenced priorities
How is it funded and sponsored? A named executive sponsor and a funding model decided up front
questions.explain: A real strategy answers these in order: an honest assessment of the current state, a target state tied to an actual business outcome, a small set of sequenced priorities for what comes first, and a funding/sponsorship model decided before the first initiative starts.

questions.prompt: A governance architecture review board's agenda for this month includes a new ADR proposing a platform change, and a request from an individual analyst for access to a single report. Per this course, which item should actually reach the board?
options: The new ADR proposing a platform change — significant, hard-to-reverse architecture decisions belong on the board's agenda
The individual access request — the board exists specifically to review and approve routine, day-to-day access
Both items equally, since the board should review every decision happening anywhere in the governance program
Neither — ADRs are filed directly with no board review of any kind
questions.explain: A review board should see new ADRs for significant, hard-to-reverse decisions. It should NOT see individual access requests or routine day-to-day decisions — those belong to the stewardship roles the operating model already assigns, and sending them to the board just creates a bottleneck.

questions.prompt: Castellan Industrial Group runs twenty plants across three regional ERPs inherited through acquisitions, with uneven data maturity by region. Per the case study, why did Castellan reject a fully centralized model and choose federated governance instead?
options: No central team could realistically own data definitions for twenty plants running three different ERPs on day one, so federated governance let each plant keep stewardship over its own operational detail while agreeing to shared standards for only the handful of enterprise-critical metrics
Federated governance was chosen because, unlike every other model, it requires no funded self-serve platform at all
Castellan rejected centralization because its plants have no cross-cutting data needs whatsoever
Castellan chose federated governance because its regulator specifically required it, the same reason Northbridge did
questions.explain: Using the selection criteria from Chapter 2, Castellan rejected a fully centralized model because no central team could realistically own definitions for twenty plants on three ERPs immediately. Federated governance fit because it let each plant retain stewardship over local detail while agreeing to shared standards for only a short list of enterprise-critical metrics — not because of a regulatory requirement, which was Northbridge's driver instead.

questions.prompt: Northbridge Financial Group centralized governance specifically for its risk and regulatory reporting domain, while keeping federated stewardship for each business line's non-regulatory data. Per the case study, what made this domain-specific centralization the right call?
options: A regulator required one accountable, traceable risk number across the whole group — exactly the kind of requirement that can't rely on three business lines independently reconciling after the fact
Northbridge centralized its risk domain purely because centralized governance is always cheaper to run than federated governance
Northbridge's business lines had no historical data silos, so centralizing cost nothing to implement
The hybrid model was chosen arbitrarily, with no specific driver named in the case study
questions.explain: Northbridge's regulator expected one accountable, traceable risk number, not three business lines independently reconciling after the fact — exactly the kind of requirement that justifies centralizing one specific domain while leaving everything else federated.

questions.prompt: Match each presentation audience to what it wants first, per this course's closing lesson on presenting governance architecture.
right: Outcome, risk, and cost in the first thirty seconds, with the diagram only after they understand why it matters
The actual design decisions and the reasoning behind them, including ADRs and rejected alternatives — the one audience that wants the diagram early
What changes for them specifically — new responsibilities, new tools, what stays the same
questions.explain: Executives want outcome, risk, and cost up front, not the diagram first. Technical peers want the actual reasoning and are the one audience that genuinely wants the diagram early. Operational teams want concrete day-to-day impact, not abstract principles.

questions.prompt: Put this course's four-part structure for presenting a governance architecture decision in the correct order.
items: Problem — stated concretely, as a specific real symptom
Impact — what it's actually costing, in terms the audience already cares about
Recommendation — the architecture decision, stated plainly, with the ADR available for more detail
Ask — the specific thing you need from this audience right now
questions.explain: The structure runs problem, impact, recommendation, ask — leading with a concrete symptom, then what it costs, then the plain recommendation, and closing with a specific, actionable ask rather than ending on "and that's our governance architecture."

questions.prompt: Select every true statement below about presenting and applying governance architecture, per this course's closing chapter.
options: Leading with the reference architecture diagram before the audience understands the problem is a common presentation mistake
The same architecture should be presented with identical ordering and depth to every audience
A presentation that ends without a specific ask wastes everyone's attendance, per this course
The seven-step practice-lab checklist includes a capabilities snapshot and an operating-model choice
Jargon like 'federated operating model' needs no translation, since every audience already knows governance terminology
questions.explain: Leading with the diagram and ending without an ask are both named mistakes. The seven-step checklist does open with a capabilities snapshot and an operating-model choice. The content should be the same architecture, but the ordering and depth should change per audience, not stay identical — and jargon does need translating for an audience that hasn't taken the earlier chapters.
